p: The games were reputed to have begun as funeral games for Melicertes, instituted by Sisyphus, the legendary king of Corinth, who found the body and buried it on the Isthmus. Another myth, probably later, held that Theseus, the legendary king of Athens, enlarged a closed night rite into athletic games dedicated to Poseidon and open to all Greeks. A further version credits Kypselos, tyrant of Corinth in the 7th century BCE, with restoring the games to their old splendour. According to Solinus they were constituted in the 49th Olympiad; 582 BCE is the date generally accepted, though one recent study places the first games in 581 BCE.

The festival was held in spring, in the second and fourth years of each Olympiad, the year before and the year after the Olympic Games, at the rural sanctuary of Poseidon on the Isthmus of Corinth, a place easily reached by land and by sea. The contests were the same as at Olympia, among them wrestling, boxing, pankration and horse and chariot racing, and there were musical and poetical contests in which women were allowed to compete.

Until at least the 5th century BCE, the time of Pindar, the victor's wreath was of celery; later it was made of pine. A victor might also be honoured with a statue or an ode, and Athens paid its own victors 100 drachmas. Before the games Corinth declared a truce that gave athletes safe passage through Greece: in 412 BCE the Athenians were invited as usual although Athens and Corinth were at war. The games were especially popular with Athenians, while the Eleans boycotted them.

The festival served many as a forum for political propaganda, and from 228 or 229 BCE Romans were allowed to take part. Corinth, rebuilt by Caesar in 44 BCE, recovered the games shortly afterwards, but they were then held in the city itself and did not return to the Isthmus until 42 or 43 CE. Libanius mentions cult activity at the Isthmus into the middle of the 4th century, and the games probably continued at least until the end of that century. The circumstances of their end are unknown; imperial pressure against pagan rites grew at that time, though some polytheistic cult practices continued at Corinth into the 6th century.
